“Well, well, Mr. Bumble,” he said at last, “there’s no denying that since the new diet was introduced, the coffins have become a little narrower and shallower. But we have to make some profit, Mr. Bumble. Properly dried timber is expensive, sir, and all the iron handles have to come by canal from Birmingham.”

“Well, well,” Mr. Bumble said, “every trade has its difficulties. A reasonable profit is certainly allowed.”

“Certainly, certainly,” the undertaker replied. “And if I don’t make a profit on one particular item, well, I make up for it in the long run, you see—he! he! he!”

“Quite right,” said Mr. Bumble.

“Though I must say,” the undertaker continued, returning to the remarks the parish officer had interrupted, “I must say, Mr. Bumble, that I face one very serious disadvantage: all the fat people die the quickest. Those who were better off and paid parish taxes for years are the first to give way when they enter the workhouse. And let me tell you, Mr. Bumble, that three or four inches more than you allowed for makes quite a hole in your profits, especially when you have a family to support, sir.”

Mr. Sowerberry said this with all the proper indignation of a badly treated man. Since Mr. Bumble felt the complaint cast some doubt on the parish’s honor, he thought it best to change the subject. Oliver Twist was foremost in his mind, so he began talking about him.

“By the way,” said Mr. Bumble, “you don’t happen to know anyone who wants a boy, do you? A parish apprentice who’s currently a dead weight—a millstone, you might say, around the parish’s throat? Generous terms, Mr. Sowerberry, generous terms.” As he spoke, Mr. Bumble raised his cane to the notice above him and tapped three times on the words “FIVE POUNDS,” printed in enormous Roman capitals.

“Good heavens!” said the undertaker, taking hold of the gold-edged lapel of Mr. Bumble’s official coat. “That’s exactly what I wanted to speak to you about. You know—my goodness, what an elegant button, Mr. Bumble! I never noticed it before.”

“Yes, I think it’s rather handsome,” said the officer, looking proudly down at the large brass buttons decorating his coat. “The design is the same as the parish seal: the Good Samaritan tending the sick and injured man. The board gave me the coat on New Year’s morning, Mr. Sowerberry. I remember wearing it for the first time at the inquest into that ruined tradesman who died in a doorway at midnight.”

Were our proud dreams to disappear like this? We had been called “a little lower than the angels,” yet we proved no better than insects that live a single day. We had named ourselves the finest of all animals, only to find we were nothing but dust. We had mourned that the pyramids outlived the preserved bodies of their builders. Yet even the shepherd’s straw hut we passed beside the road was built to last longer than the entire human race. How could we reconcile this terrible change with our former ambitions and our apparent powers?

Suddenly a voice within me seemed to speak, clear and distinct: This was determined from eternity. Since the empty universe first gave birth, the horses carrying Time forward have been bound to this hour and this outcome. Would you reverse the unchanging laws of Necessity?

Mother of the world! Servant of the Almighty! Eternal, unchanging Necessity, whose busy fingers forever weave the unbreakable chain of events—I will not complain of what you do. My human mind may be unable to accept that everything that happens is right. But since what happens must happen, I will sit among the ruins and smile. Truly, we were born not to enjoy life, but to submit and to hope.

Would the reader grow tired if I described every detail of our long journey from Paris to Geneva? If I recorded each day’s mounting miseries in a journal, could my hand write them all down? Could language express the many forms of our suffering, with one dreadful event pressing close upon the next? Be patient, reader, whoever and wherever you are. Whether you are a spirit or a human descended from some surviving couple and living on earth, you will read here about the deeds of an extinct race. You will wonder whether those who endured these things were made of flesh as fragile, of bodies as delicate, as your own. Indeed they were. Weep for them, then. Surely, solitary creature, you will be gentle. Shed tears of pity, but keep listening to the story and learn what those who came before you did and suffered.

Yet the final events of our journey through France held such strange horror and dark misery that I dare not linger over them. If I examined each incident, every fraction of a second would hold a devastating story, whose smallest word would chill the blood in your young veins. It is right for me to build this memorial to the vanished race so that you may learn from it. But I should not drag you through hospital wards or the hidden rooms where the dead are kept.

The only question that seemed to trouble him was whom to kill. He understood that murder, like the religions of the ancient pagan world, needs a victim as well as a priest. Since he was no genius, he had no enemies. Besides, he felt this was no occasion for satisfying a personal grudge or dislike: his mission was far too solemn and serious for that. He therefore wrote a list of his friends and relatives on a sheet of notepaper. After careful thought, he chose Lady Clementina Beauchamp, a dear old lady who lived in Curzon Street and was his second cousin on his mother’s side. He had always been very fond of Lady Clem, as everyone called her. And because he was extremely wealthy himself, having inherited all Lord Rugby’s property when he came of age, he could gain no vulgar financial advantage from her death. Indeed, the more he considered it, the more she seemed exactly the right person. Feeling that any delay would be unfair to Sybil, he decided to make the arrangements immediately.

First, of course, he had to pay the palm reader. He sat down at a small Sheraton writing table near the window and wrote a check for £105 payable to Mr. Septimus Podgers. He put it in an envelope and instructed his valet to deliver it to West Moon Street. Then he telephoned the stables for his hansom cab and dressed to go out. As he left the room, he looked back at Sybil Merton’s photograph. Whatever happened, he vowed, he would never let her discover what he was doing for her. He would always keep the secret of his self-sacrifice buried in his heart.

On his way to the Buckingham, he stopped at a florist’s and sent Sybil a beautiful basket of narcissus flowers, with lovely white petals and bright centers like pheasants’ eyes. When he reached the club, he went directly to the library, rang the bell, and asked the waiter for a lemon and soda and a book about poisons. He had firmly decided that poison was the best way to handle this troublesome business. Any kind of physical violence was deeply unpleasant to him. He was also particularly anxious to avoid killing Lady Clementina in a way that might draw public attention. He hated the thought of being treated as a celebrity at Lady Windermere’s parties, or of finding his name in the gossip columns of vulgar society newspapers.
